title: Buying Whisky at Duty Free | Craft Beer School
desc: Buying whisky at duty free: how to tell a real saving, India's allowance on arrival, liquids rules on connections and how travel retail exclusives compare.
teaser: Duty free is not always cheaper. Here is how to tell in the two minutes before boarding.
standfirst: Airport whisky shelves promise savings. Sometimes they deliver, especially for Indians used to high state taxes. Sometimes the bottle costs less at home. Here is how to judge quickly and carry it home legally.
sections: Duty free removes tax, not the margin

Duty free shops sell without the local excise duties and sales taxes. The saving is biggest when your home taxes are high, which in India they usually are. But airport shops pay high rents and still take a margin, so the price is not simply the shelf price minus tax.

Compare by the litre, not by the bottle. Travel retail often sells 1 litre bottles, while Indian shelves use 750 ml and European shelves usually 700 ml. A bottle that looks only slightly dearer may hold a third more whisky.
Know your allowance before you queue

India's baggage rules limit how much alcohol an adult arriving from abroad can bring in free of duty. For several years the limit has been two litres. Rules change, so check the current position on the CBIC website before you fly. Over the allowance, you pay duty at the airport. It is not cheap.

Most major Indian international airports have arrival duty free shops. Buying there means you carry nothing through security on the way and can check your allowance on the spot.
Your state has a say too

Clearing customs is not the end of it. Liquor is a state subject in India, so the state you take the bottle home to also has rules on how much you may possess and bring in. Prohibition states such as Gujarat and Bihar are strict. Other states have limits of their own.

If you are flying into one state and travelling on to another, check both. A bottle bought legally at the airport can still be a problem at a state border.

Cabin bags are limited to small containers of liquid at security, usually 100 ml each. Duty free bought airside is sealed in a tamper-evident bag with the receipt inside. Keep it sealed until your final destination.

If your connection involves another security screening, some airports may still refuse liquids from an earlier duty free purchase. The safest plan is to buy at the last airport before home or at arrival duty free. If you buy at departure, check the rules for your connecting airport.
Travel retail exclusives are not always a bargain

Many duty free shelves carry bottlings made only for travel retail, often without an age statement and with grand names. Some are excellent. Some are standard whisky in a smarter box. A missing age statement is not a fault in itself, but it does mean you are judging blind.

Read the label for cask type, strength and whether the whisky is chill filtered or coloured. Our guide to whisky age statements explains what the numbers on a label do and do not tell you.
Do your homework before the gate

Make a short list before you travel. Note the price at home of two or three whiskies you would happily buy. At the shop, compare per litre and check whether the exclusive bottling on offer is really different from what you can get at home.

Counter tastings help, but you are about to board or land. Keep any tasting to a small sip, drink water and never drive after landing if you have been tasting. Long flights are tiring enough without a head full of samples.

Familiar brands in litre bottles are usually the most reliable saving. You know the whisky, you know its home price and the extra 250 ml is easy to value.
Packing it for the trip home

If the whisky goes in checked baggage rather than the cabin, wrap the bottle in clothes and seal it in a plastic bag in case of breakage. Keep it upright if the box allows. Keep the receipt; customs may ask for it on arrival.

Airline safety rules also apply. Spirits above 70% ABV are generally not allowed on aircraft at all. Airlines also limit how much strong alcohol each passenger may carry in checked bags. Normal bottling strengths and most cask strength whiskies fall well inside those limits, but check your airline's rules if you are bringing back several bottles.

Whisky does not age in the bottle, so there is no rush to open it and no benefit in keeping it for years. Store it upright, away from heat and sunlight. Our guide to whisky in the duty free channel covers the business side of travel retail.
Price one bottle before your next trip

Before your next international flight, choose one whisky you like. Note its MRP in your state and convert it to a price per litre. At the airport, do the same with the duty free price.

That single comparison tells you whether duty free is a real saving for you. Keep the note for next time.
faqs: How much whisky can I bring into India duty free?
The baggage rules set a limit for adult passengers, which for several years has been two litres of alcohol. Check the current rules on the CBIC website before you travel.
Can I carry duty free whisky on a connecting flight?
Keep it sealed in the tamper-evident bag with the receipt. Some airports still refuse liquids at a second screening, so buying at the final airport or on arrival is safest.
Is duty free whisky always cheaper?
No. Compare price per litre with your home price. In high-tax Indian states the saving is often real, but not always.
